findings.source_passage: the doubloon is mine, Fate reserved the doubloon for me. _I_ only; none of ye could have raised the White Whale first.
findings.source_locator: paragraph 8, Ahab's speech after Tashtego's claim
findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'Fate reserved the doubloon for me. _I_ only' is the chapter's first explicit articulation of Ahab's fatalist theology; it is interpretively indispensable and critically discussed as the hinge between predestination and agency. The draft drops 'Fate reserved the doubloon for me' and 'none of ye could have raised the White Whale first,' gutting the fatalist claim.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore verbatim: 'the doubloon is mine, Fate reserved the doubloon for me. _I_ only; none of ye could have raised the White Whale first.' — this must appear in Ahab's speech after Tashtego's interjection.

findings.source_passage: Man, man! did I not know thee brave as fearless fire (and as mechanical) I could swear thou wert a poltroon.
findings.source_locator: paragraph near end, Ahab's rebuke of Stubb at the wrecked boat
findings.why_it_matters: The parenthetical '(and as mechanical)' is one of the most critically cited phrases in the chapter — it encapsulates Ahab's view of Stubb as instinct without consciousness, and the ironic 'brave as fearless fire' is a signature rhetorical shape. The draft skips directly from the opening rebuke to 'Groan nor laugh should be heard before a wreck,' erasing this entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore: 'Man, man! did I not know thee brave as fearless fire (and as mechanical) I could swear thou wert a poltroon.' between the opening rebuke and the closing sentence.

findings.source_passage: The day was nearly done; only the hem of his golden robe was rustling.
findings.source_locator: penultimate section, just before 'Can't see the spout now, sir'
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence is prosodically singular — one of the most anthologized incidental lines in the novel, functioning as a lyric marker of approaching doom. The draft replaces it with the flat 'Dusk fell,' erasing its register entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace 'Dusk fell' with the source sentence verbatim: 'The day was nearly done; only the hem of his golden robe was rustling.'

findings.source_passage: Cold, cold—I shiver!—How now? Aloft there! D'ye see him? Sing out for every spout, though he spout ten times a second!
findings.source_locator: after 'Ahab stands alone among the millions of the peopled earth, nor gods nor men his neighbors!'
findings.why_it_matters: The sudden physical confession 'Cold, cold—I shiver!' breaks Ahab's rhetorical register with a flash of involuntary vulnerability — a critically noted moment of psychic exposure immediately suppressed by the command to the mast-heads. Its excision flattens the tonal complexity of the speech's ending.
findings.suggested_fix: Append after 'nor gods nor men his neighbors!': 'Cold, cold—I shiver!—How now? Aloft there! D'ye see him? Sing out for every spout, though he spout ten times a second!'

findings.source_passage: So, in a gale, the but half baffled Channel billows only recoil from the base of the Eddystone, triumphantly to overleap its summit with their scud.
findings.why_it_matters: This extended simile gives Moby Dick's pitchpoling a monumental geographic analogy; it is textually distinctive in rhythm and imagery and reinforces the whale's sublime implacability. Its omission strips a key Melvillean register marker from the action sequence.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore after the pitchpoling description: 'So, in a gale, the but half baffled Channel billows only recoil from the base of the Eddystone, triumphantly to overleap its summit with their scud.'

summary: Two high-severity losses (Ahab's fatalist doubloon speech and the '(and as mechanical)' rebuke of Stubb) and three medium-severity losses ('only the hem of his golden robe,' 'Cold, cold—I shiver!,' and the Eddystone simile) require regeneration.
